title: A full-wave Method-of-Moments solver for an agentic antenna-design pipeline
desc: Wrote an RWG/EFIE boundary-element solver from scratch (NumPy + Gmsh), validated it against the Mie series and the half-wave dipole, debugged three failures that masqueraded as physics, and wrapped it into an optimize → verify → calibrate loop so an LLM-driven antenna designer has to answer to Maxwell's equations.
heroCaption: meandered inverted-F antenna: conforming surface mesh (left) and surface current density near resonance (right)
body:
status: working, 20 tests · stack: python, numpy, scipy, gmsh · ~3,000 lines · code on github

I had an antenna-design pipeline that could optimize, but could not check its own answers. This is the story of giving it a full-wave electromagnetic solver written from scratch, validating that solver against closed-form physics, finding three bugs that each looked like physics until they were isolated, and then wrapping the solver into a loop that forces every optimizer result to answer to Maxwell's equations before an engineer sees it.

1. The problem

The pipeline (an LLM agent plus a Python library) designs small antennas for implants and wearables: meandered inverted-F antennas, PIFAs, loops, patches. It has parametric templates for each family, a CMA-ES / Bayesian optimizer, matching-network synthesis, SAR checks, and a Streamlit front end. What it did not have was physics. Every template carried a closed-form estimate of its resonance and input impedance (a quarter-wave length with an effective permittivity, a radiation resistance that scales with height squared, a parallel-RLC shape around resonance), and the optimizer ran thousands of evaluations against those formulas. The full-wave solver entries in the UI, OpenEMS and NEC2, were never wired in; selecting them printed a warning and fell back to the formulas.

The templates' own docstrings put their accuracy at ±20–30 % on resonance. For an RF engineer that is a starting point, not a deliverable. I wanted a solver that runs in seconds on a laptop, needs no external EM package, speaks the geometry the pipeline already produces, and is honest about what it does not model.

2. Choosing the method

The structures are thin conductors: copper traces on a plane, plates, vertical feed and shorting pins. A surface integral-equation method is the natural fit. Instead of discretizing a volume around the antenna (FDTD, FEM) you discretize only the metal, the radiation condition is built into the Green's function, and a few hundred unknowns describe a complete antenna. The price is a dense matrix, but for a few thousand unknowns a dense LU factorization is a fraction of a second.

The formulation is the electric-field integral equation (EFIE) with Rao–Wilton–Glisson (RWG) basis functions on a triangular mesh. On a perfect conductor the tangential electric field vanishes, so the scattered field produced by the unknown surface current \(\mathbf J\) must cancel the tangential impressed field:

\[ \hat n \times \Big[\, j\omega\mu_0 \!\int_S \mathbf J(\mathbf r')\,G\,dS' \;-\; \frac{1}{j\omega\varepsilon_0}\nabla\!\int_S \nabla'\!\cdot\mathbf J(\mathbf r')\,G\,dS' \Big] = \hat n \times \mathbf E^{\,i}(\mathbf r), \qquad G=\frac{e^{-jkR}}{4\pi R}. \]

Expanding \(\mathbf J=\sum_n I_n \mathbf f_n\) in RWG functions (each lives on a pair of triangles sharing an edge and carries unit current across that edge) and testing with the same functions gives the dense linear system \(\mathbf Z\mathbf I=\mathbf V\) with

\[ Z_{mn}= jk\eta\left[\iint \mathbf f_m\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_n\,G\,dS'dS \;-\; \frac{1}{k^2}\iint (\nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_m)(\nabla'\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_n)\,G\,dS'dS\right]. \]

Everything difficult about the method is in evaluating those double integrals: the kernel is singular when the two triangles coincide, nearly singular when they touch, and smooth but oscillatory when they are far apart. Get that wrong and you do not get slightly wrong answers; you get spurious resonances that look exactly like real ones.

3. Architecture

Seven modules, about 1,200 lines for the solver:

modulejobthe non-obvious part
layout.pyAntennaGeometry → flat conductor panels + delta-gap lineschains planar trace segments into mitred ribbon polygons; turns thin conductor boxes into one plate on the face that looks at the rest of the structure; vertical pins become ribbons whose width direction follows the trace they land on; a port becomes a gap line, with a bridging ribbon when the port spans free space. All coordinates are snapped so 35 µm copper thickness never becomes a sliver face.
gmsh_mesher.pyconforming triangulationOpenCASCADE fragment of every panel and line together, per-panel size fields with distance-based grading, structured (transfinite) meshes on ribbons, a triangle-quality gate with multi-algorithm retry.
mesh.pySurfaceMesh, RWG connectivityan edge shared by k ≥ 3 triangles (a pin meeting a plate) gets k−1 basis functions paired with the first triangle, which preserves Kirchhoff continuity at the junction without special junction bases.
quadrature.py · analytic.pyDunavant rules; closed-form \(\int_T dS'/R\) and \(\int_T \mathbf r' dS'/R\)the singular integrals are done exactly as sums over the three edges of the source triangle.
efie.pymatrix fillsparse basis matrices around a dense kernel; static part computed once per mesh, only the smooth remainder refilled per frequency.
excitation.py · postprocess.pyports, plane waves, far field, RCS, conductor lossstrip delta gap: \(V_m = V_0 l_m\) on every RWG edge crossing the gap line, \(Z_{in}=V_0/\sum I_m l_m\).
solver.pyMoMSolver, same interface as the existing analytical solverfrequency sweep, Y→S conversion for multi-port structures, diagnostics (power balance, mesh size in wavelengths, what was not modelled).

4. Building the numerics, bottom up

4.1 Quadrature and the singular integrals

Integration over triangles uses symmetric Gauss (Dunavant) rules in barycentric coordinates: 1, 3, 6 and 7 points, exact to polynomial degree 1, 2, 4 and 5. The first test I wrote checks every rule against \(\int_T \lambda_1^a\lambda_2^b\,dA = a!\,b!\,2A/(a+b+2)!\) for all monomials up to its degree; they pass to 10⁻¹⁵.

Sampling \(1/R\) with any such rule fails when the observation point is on or near the source triangle. So the kernel is split, \(G = \frac{1}{4\pi R} + \frac{e^{-jkR}-1}{4\pi R}\): the second term is smooth everywhere (its limit at \(R\to0\) is \(-jk/4\pi\)) and can be sampled; the first is integrated in closed form. For an observation point \(\mathbf r\) at signed height \(d\) above the plane of triangle \(T\), with \(P^0_i\) the signed distance from the projection of \(\mathbf r\) to edge \(i\), \(l^\pm_i\) the signed positions of the edge endpoints along the edge, and \(R^\pm_i\) the distances to them,

\[ \int_T \frac{dS'}{R} = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\left[ P^0_i \ln\frac{R^+_i+l^+_i}{R^-_i+l^-_i} \;-\; |d|\left(\tan^{-1}\frac{P^0_i l^+_i}{(R^0_i)^2+|d|R^+_i} - \tan^{-1}\frac{P^0_i l^-_i}{(R^0_i)^2+|d|R^-_i}\right)\right], \]

with a companion formula for the vector integral \(\int_T (\mathbf r'-\boldsymbol\rho)/R\,dS'\). The logarithm has two algebraically equal forms, \(\ln\frac{R^++l^+}{R^-+l^-}\) and \(\ln\frac{R^--l^-}{R^+-l^+}\), and only one of them is numerically stable depending on which side of the edge the point projects to; picking the wrong one gives 0/0 for points on the edge's extension. I tested the implementation against adaptive double integration at five observation points (inside, above, outside in-plane, off-plane) to eight digits, and it stays finite where the numerical integral diverges.

4.2 Assembling Z without loops

Written naively, the fill is a quadruple loop over test and source triangles and their quadrature points. I wrote it instead as sparse matrices around one dense kernel. If \(F_c\) is the sparse matrix whose entry \([(t,i),n]\) holds \(W_{ti}\,f_n(\mathbf r_{ti})_c\) (quadrature weight times the c-component of basis n at point i of triangle t) and \(D\) holds \(W_{ti}\,\nabla\!\cdot\!\mathbf f_n\), then

\[ \mathbf A=\sum_{c\in\{x,y,z\}} F_c^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbb G\,F_c,\qquad \boldsymbol\Phi = D^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbb G\, D,\qquad \mathbf Z = jk\eta\left(\mathbf A - \boldsymbol\Phi/k^2\right), \]

where \(\mathbb G\) is the kernel sampled between all pairs of quadrature points. That matrix is computed in row blocks and never stored whole. The near pairs (centroid distance under three element sizes) have their \(1/R\) part zeroed in \(\mathbb G\) and replaced by the closed-form integrals at the basis level; when the test triangle is much larger than the source triangle, the test triangle is subdivided into 4, 16 or 64 sub-triangles for that outer integral because the inner potential is sharply peaked there. Everything frequency-independent (the static kernel, the analytic near terms, the Gram matrix for conductor loss) is computed once per mesh; per frequency only the smooth remainder is sampled, with a cheaper 3-point rule. A 21-point sweep on an 800-unknown antenna takes about two seconds.

Conductor loss enters as a Leontovich surface impedance \(Z_s=(1+j)\sqrt{\omega\mu_0/2\sigma}\), halved because a sheet carries current on both faces, added to the diagonal blocks through the same Gram matrix. Because \(k\) and \(\eta\) are complex throughout, a lossy homogeneous background medium (muscle at 400 MHz: εr 57, σ 0.8 S/m) costs nothing extra.

4.3 Ports and post-processing

Feeds are strip delta gaps: a line across a conductor where a 1 V source is impressed. Every RWG edge lying on that line gets \(V_m=\pm V_0 l_m\), with the sign chosen so all of them push current in the port direction, and the terminal current is \(\sum \pm I_m l_m\). For multi-port structures each port is driven in turn with the others shorted, which gives the Y matrix directly, then Z and S. The far field comes from the radiation vector \(\mathbf N(\hat r)=\sum_i W_i\mathbf J_i e^{jk\hat r\cdot\mathbf r_i}\) on a 37 × 73 sphere grid; integrating the radiation intensity gives \(P_{rad}\), and comparing it with \(\tfrac12\mathrm{Re}(V_0 I^*)\) gives a power-balance number that every run reports. For a lossless conductor it must be 1.000, and the solver prints it precisely so that a user never has to trust a number they cannot check.

5. Validation against things with known answers

Before touching a single antenna template I ran the solver on structures with analytical references. A solver that has not been validated this way is a random-number generator with a colorbar.

5.1 The half-wave strip dipole

5.2 Scattering from a sphere, against the Mie series

The dipole exercises the feed model as much as the matrix. To test the matrix alone I meshed a PEC sphere with Gmsh, illuminated it with a plane wave (the excitation vector is then just \(F^{\mathsf T}\) applied to the incident field samples) and compared the backscatter cross-section with the exact Mie series, which I implemented from spherical Bessel functions in a dozen lines. The two agree within 0.35 dB across ka from 0.6 to 3 on a λ/10 mesh (1,068 unknowns), including through the resonance-region oscillations.

5.3 Small loops against the textbook inductance

5.4 Reciprocity and energy

Two more tests run on every commit: a two-port pair of dipoles at λ/6 spacing must give \(S_{21}=S_{12}\) to 10⁻³, and a copper dipole must satisfy \((P_{rad}+P_{loss})/P_{in}=1\) to 1 % while radiating less than 100 % of its input. These are cheap, and they are exactly the invariants that break first when a sign or a factor of two goes wrong in the fill.

6. From templates to meshes

The pipeline's templates emit traces (start, end, width), boxes (ground planes, patches, substrates) and ports. Turning that into a mesh a boundary-element solver can use is where most of the engineering went.

Meshing rules that came out of the design/test cycles: one element across a strip narrower than λ/40, two across wider ones; plates at λ/10 but never coarser than twice the spacing to the nearest parallel conductor (a patch 5 mm above ground meshed at 10 mm gave nonsense); grading fields from every fine panel into its coarse neighbours so element sizes never jump by more than about 2×; and the k−1 rule for junction edges so a pin can meet a plate anywhere on its surface.

7. Three bugs that looked like physics

The validation cases passed on the first try. The templates did not: the MIFA showed a comb of narrow resonances at 525, 540, 570 and 640 MHz, far below its first physical resonance, and the PIFA's impedance jumped between 11 Ω and 219 Ω from one 50 MHz step to the next. Each of the three causes took a controlled experiment to find.

7.1 The symmetric solve

The Galerkin EFIE matrix is symmetric in exact arithmetic (reciprocity), so I had used SciPy's symmetric LDLᵀ path. But the numerical matrix is only symmetric to about 10⁻³, because near-pair integrals are evaluated with the test integral on one triangle and the analytic integral on the other, and the two orderings do not produce identical numbers. An LDLᵀ solver reads only one triangle of the matrix and silently assumes the other. On a well-conditioned mesh the 10⁻³ inconsistency is harmless; on a graded mesh with condition number 10⁷ it is amplified into spurious near-null vectors, which show up as resonances.

The experiment that found it: identical matrix, two solvers. Then I confirmed that a 6-point and a 7-point static quadrature rule, which differ only in their asymmetry error, gave impedances differing by 700 Ω with LDLᵀ and by 0.004 Ω with LU. The fix is two lines: symmetrize \(\mathbf Z\leftarrow(\mathbf Z+\mathbf Z^{\mathsf T})/2\), which is legitimate because the true operator is reciprocal, then a full LU.

7.2 The end caps

When the layout code turned a trace into a ribbon polygon, it added square caps of half a width at each end so that touching chains would overlap and fuse. On a 0.5 mm MIFA trace that is 0.25 mm and invisible. On the 10 mm-wide validation dipole it is 5 mm at each end, 7 % more length, and the Gmsh-meshed dipole resonated at 0.433 λ instead of 0.465 λ. I spent an afternoon suspecting the unstructured mesh. The fix was to make ribbons flush and let pins share the ribbon's end edge instead.

7.3 The CAD kernel does not imprint touching faces

A vertical pin meeting a plate must share mesh edges with it or current cannot flow. I relied on OpenCASCADE's boolean fragment to imprint the pin's edge into the plate face. It does so for lines, and for faces that cross, but not reliably for a face that merely touches another along an edge inside it. The pin looked connected in a 3D view and was electrically floating.

The first fix, explicitly embedding the pin's boundary curves into the host face, connected the pin but created a new failure at finer mesh sizes: the mesher, given the same constraint twice (a fragmented line and an embedded curve at the same location, plus a 1D node that happened to land on the pin's corner), produced cascades of zero-area triangles that halved in size at each step. The final fix fragments the pin's end edges as explicit lines and inserts their endpoints as vertices of the host polygon, removes the embed step entirely, meshes ribbons with structured transfinite grids, merges nodes closer than 10⁻³ of an element, and rejects any mesh whose minimum triangle quality \(4\sqrt3 A/\sum l^2\) falls under 0.08 before retrying with another algorithm. All seven templates now mesh cleanly from refinement 1.0 down to 0.5.

7.4 Proof the fixes worked: convergence

8. What it costs

9. Closing the loop: the fidelity ladder

With a solver I could trust, the question became how to use it. It is too slow to sit inside the optimizer's thousands of evaluations, so I put it around the optimizer instead.

  1. Verify. verify_design runs the closed-form model and the full-wave solver on the same geometry and produces a report: full-wave resonances, S11 and impedance at target, bandwidth, efficiency, gain, mesh size in wavelengths, power balance, a graded agreement, and a list of what was not modelled. The comparison is like-for-like: if the design has a substrate, the closed-form model is re-evaluated with εr = 1 so the discrepancy measures model error rather than the missing dielectric.
  2. Converge. A second solve on a 0.7× mesh reports how far the resonance and |Z| moved.
  3. Calibrate. The template is wrapped so its closed-form resonance and resistance are scaled to the full-wave values. Geometry, parameter bounds and optimizers are untouched; only the fast surrogate changes.
  4. Repeat. Optimize on the calibrated surrogate, verify, recalibrate. A millisecond connectivity check (does every pin end land on a conductor, does the port cut one) runs inside the optimizer as a penalty, because the first ladder run caught the optimizer placing the PIFA's feed pin outside the patch, a design the closed-form model was happy with and the full-wave solver correctly saw as an open circuit.

The ladder surfaced something more useful than a scale factor. Running it five times on an air PIFA at 2.45 GHz, the closed-form model's error swung from −44 % to +17 % between candidate designs. The error is not a constant, so no global calibration can remove it, and the ladder now says so in its output and reports the best verified round instead of the last one. The honest conclusion is that the final refinement of a design belongs to the full-wave solver, which is the first item on the roadmap below.

10. Implants: what happens in tissue

Far field and efficiency are deliberately not reported in a lossy medium: radiated power is not defined without a boundary to integrate over, and printing a number there would be a lie.

11. Where it lives

The solver implements the same interface as the pipeline's analytical solver, so it drops into the optimizer's objective unchanged. It is exposed three ways: as agent tools (simulate_fullwave, verify_fullwave, fidelity_ladder, with the system prompt now making verification a mandatory phase), as a CLI (python app.py verify -t pifa -f 2000), and in the Streamlit UI, where selecting the full-wave solver shows the S11 overlay against the closed-form model, the graded agreement, the diagnostics, the surface-current map on the mesh, and the full-wave 3D gain pattern. Gmsh installs its own signal handlers, which fail inside a Streamlit worker thread; that was a one-argument fix once found.

12. Limits, stated plainly

No dielectrics. The solver models conductors in a homogeneous medium. A substrate-loaded design resonates lower in reality by roughly \(1-1/\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r,eff}}\), and every report prints that range. For a thin substrate under an antenna in air this is a mild error; for a patch on FR-4 it is not, and the tool should be read as air-substrate physics until layered-media Green's functions are implemented.
  • Thin sheets only; thick blocks are meshed as closed shells, and closed shells carry EFIE interior resonances at discrete frequencies (a combined-field formulation would remove them).
  • Oblique 3D wires (the helix template) are refused with a message; a wire-kernel solver is the right tool there.
  • Dense O(N²) storage; about 8,000 unknowns is the practical ceiling on a laptop.
  • In a lossy medium only the input impedance is produced.

13. What I would build next

  • Layered-media Green's function (spectral-domain, discrete complex images) for substrates and skin/fat/muscle stacks. This removes the biggest caveat and is the difference between a verification tool and a design tool for implants.
  • Two-antenna links. The multi-port path already works; an implant and an external reader in one impedance matrix gives \(S_{21}\) directly, a physics-based link budget instead of Friis with assumed gains.
  • Full-wave in the loop on the optimizer's top candidates, now that the ladder has shown the surrogate's error is not a constant.
  • A compiled kernel (Numba or C++) for the fill, which is embarrassingly parallel and would push the ceiling past 20,000 unknowns.
  • Chaining into measurement. The pipeline already calibrates simulation against VNA data; the ladder should end at the bench, full-wave → measured S1P → corrected model.

14. What I took from it

The physics was the easy part; the classical formulation has been settled since the 1980s and it worked on the first validation case. The hard part, and the part I would not have believed without doing it, is that every one of the failures I hit produced output that looked like antenna physics: resonances at plausible frequencies, impedance curves with the right shape, efficiencies between 0 and 1. The only things that separated a bug from a result were invariants I could compute independently (power balance, reciprocity, Mie, refinement convergence) and experiments that changed one thing at a time. A solver without those is not a solver.

title: ViPO: rewarding the step that keeps a problem solvable
desc: Step-level RL for Countdown arithmetic with an exact reachability oracle as the reward: a legal move is rewarded only if a solution still exists after it. Sound and complete labels, a provable exponential credit-assignment gap over terminal rewards, Pass@1 0.884 vs RLOO's 0.618 at 33× fewer training tokens, plus my own analysis showing 80 % of legal Countdown moves are dead and an oracle you can play with in the page.
heroCaption: how hazardous Countdown is: on a solvable instance only one legal first move in five keeps the target reachable, and the greedy 'closest to target' move is dead 53 % of the time
body:
with Sandra Yang · Stanford · Qwen2.5-0.5B on Countdown · trained on a single H100 via Modal · checkpoint rohkymntn/vpo-a-countdown-qwen-200step

Most reasoning failures I see in small language models are not illegal steps. They are perfectly legal steps that quietly delete the only remaining path to the answer. A terminal reward cannot tell the model which step did that. This project asks what happens when the reward is placed exactly at that step instead, and answers it with a proof, a training run, two ablations, and a failure mode.

0.884
Pass@1, VPO-R (RLOO: 0.618)
33×
fewer training tokens than RLOO

theorems: sound, complete, exponential gap

of legal Countdown moves are dead (my analysis, §7)

1. The problem: legal is not the same as alive

Countdown gives a model a few numbers, say [3, 4, 6, 8], and a target, say 24. It must combine the numbers with +, −, ×, ÷, each number used once, until one value equals the target. Every step removes two numbers and adds their result, so the state is just the multiset of what is left. A step like 8 − 6 = 2 is arithmetically fine and looks like progress, and from [2, 3, 4] the target is still reachable (2 × 3 × 4). The step 8 + 6 = 14 is exactly as legal and looks exactly as reasonable, and from [3, 4, 14] no combination reaches 24 at all. Whether a step was good depends on a question the model is never asked: after taking it, does a solution still exist? One of those two moves ended the game two steps before the final answer was written down, and nothing in the trace says which.

Supervised fine-tuning imitates one demonstration and never sees the alternatives. DPO and IPO compare two complete responses. RLOO scores the final answer with a verifier. All three place the learning signal on the whole trace, so when a six-step trace fails because step two killed the search space, the gradient has to guess which step to blame. On a branching problem that guess is statistically expensive, and I could prove how expensive.

2. The idea: reward the transition, not the trace

The state graph of Countdown is finite and small. That makes a quantity computable that is usually only estimable: whether a state is still solvable. Define the residual horizon of a state \(s\) for target \(y\) by dynamic programming over multisets of rationals,

\[ d_y(s)=\begin{cases}0 & s\ni y\\ 1+\min_{a\in\mathcal A(s)} d_y(T(s,a)) & |s|>1\\ \infty & |s|=1,\ s\not\ni y\end{cases}\qquad \mathrm{Alive}_y(s)=\mathbf 1[d_y(s)<\infty]. \]

The viability label of an action is simply the aliveness of the state it leads to, \(z_y(s,a)=\mathrm{Alive}_y(T(s,a))\), and the per-step reward is 1 for an alive step, a small \(\rho=0.1\) for a legal-but-dead step, and 0 for anything unparseable or arithmetically wrong. Exact rational arithmetic makes division unambiguous, and memoization makes the oracle essentially free: a typical solvable 4-number instance has about twenty alive states in total.

Training is self-play with a group-relative policy gradient. At each state the policy samples \(G=8\) candidate next steps, the oracle labels each, and the leave-one-out advantage \(A_i=r_i-\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{j\ne i}r_j\) drives

\[ \mathcal L(\theta)=-\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^G A_i\log\pi_\theta(\hat a_i\mid p(s,h))+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})-\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}\widehat H(\pi_\theta). \]

The update is the same shape as RLOO. What changed is only what is being rewarded: a transition property instead of a terminal score. The rollout then advances along a sampled alive step (or, early in training when the policy cannot find one, an oracle-supplied alive step, never at test time) so that later states are visited from the start.

3. What can be proven

Because the oracle is exact, the labels come with guarantees rather than reward-model error.

  • Sound and complete. \(z_y(s,a)=1\) if and only if a legal continuation after \(a\) reaches the goal. This is the definition unwound: the continuation is exactly the witness.
  • Staying alive solves. If the start state is alive and a deterministic policy chooses an alive action at every nonterminal state, it reaches the goal in at most \(m-1\) steps. Each action shrinks the multiset by one, every reached state is alive by induction, and an alive single-element state can only be the target. The corollary is the sharp one: a dead transition is irrecoverable, no future policy can save the instance.
  • Exponential credit-assignment separation. On a depth-\(H\), branching-\(B\) search where exactly one action stays alive at each level and reward is given only at the end, deciding whether a fixed root action is alive from terminal-only random rollouts needs \(N=\Omega\!\left(B^{H-1}\log(1/\delta)\right)\) samples to see a single success with probability \(1-\delta\). One oracle query decides it. The proof is two lines: the success probability of a random continuation is \(p=B^{-(H-1)}\) and \((1-p)^N\le\delta\) forces \(N\ge\log(1/\delta)/(-\log(1-p))=\Theta(p^{-1}\log(1/\delta))\).

4. Setup: one seed, one verifier, two budgets

Every method starts from the same SFT seed, a Qwen2.5-0.5B fine-tuned on Countdown demonstrations, and is scored by the same rule-based evaluator (1.0 for a valid equation using each number once, 0.1 for well-formed but wrong, 0.0 for unparseable). VPO trains for 200 self-play updates (batch 8, \(G=8\), lr \(10^{-5}\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}=10^{-3}\), temperature 0.8) on one H100, alternating a vLLM sampling worker and a PyTorch update worker that hand off through on-disk checkpoints because they cannot share the GPU. Evaluation is on a fresh held-out set of 500 problems with 16 rollouts per prompt, reporting Pass@k with 95 % Wilson intervals.

The same checkpoint is evaluated two ways. VPO-A samples candidate steps and takes the first legal one, with no oracle at test time: this is what the policy learned. VPO-R samples candidates and lets the oracle's viability label pick an alive one: this is a diagnostic upper bound on how much signal the label carries at inference, not a second model.

Because the two rewards give different kinds of feedback, I tracked two cost budgets instead of one: the number of reward labels (oracle or verifier calls) and the number of training output tokens generated. RLOO: about 102,400 labels and 50.7 M tokens. VPO: about 64,000 labels and 1.54 M tokens, because a labeled sample is a single step string rather than a full answer.

5. Results

methodpass@1 [95 % CI]pass@8pass@16mean score
SFT seed0.322 [.283, .364]0.8040.8880.377

Two honest readings of that table. The trained weights alone (0.486) still trail RLOO (0.618) on Pass@1; the headline improvement over RLOO comes from reranking with the oracle at test time. And VPO-R with the oracle approaches the SFT seed's Pass@16 ceiling (0.888) with a single reranked answer, which is the more useful way to state the gain: the viability signal converts sixteen samples' worth of search into one.

5.1 Training dynamics

6. Ablations: where the gain comes from, and where it breaks

Why does the aggressive repair rule blow up? My reading is that it changes the sampling distribution of the group away from the policy just where the advantage is computed, so the leave-one-out baseline is contaminated by actions the policy did not produce, and late in training, when most candidates are already alive and the occasional bad one triggers a replacement, the gradient starts pushing probability toward tokens the policy never emitted. It is the same lesson as importance-weight blow-ups in off-policy RL, arriving through a side door.

7. Investigating the premise: how hazardous is Countdown, really?

The whole method rests on the claim that legal-but-dead moves are common and hard to spot. I wanted a number, so I reimplemented the residual oracle from scratch (exact rational DP over canonicalized multisets, memoized) and ran it over 3,000 uniformly random 4-number instances with numbers and targets in 1–99. The script and its output are next to this page.

That last number is the one that matters. "Get closer to the target" is precisely the heuristic a fluent model learns from demonstrations, and it kills the instance more often than not. A few of the cases the analysis pulled out:

numbers → targetgreedy move (closest to target)alive moves instead
[2, 8, 12, 71] → 938 × 12 = 96 · dead2 + 8, 2 + 12, 2 + 71, 8 + 12 …
[19, 29, 31, 70] → 5829 + 31 = 60 · dead31 − 19 = 12, 19 + 70 = 89 …
[25, 32, 43, 81] → 381 ÷ 25 · dead32 + 43 = 75 (the only one)
[24, 25, 31, 38] → 2438 − 24 = 14 · deadanything that leaves the 24 alone

The paper's training set samples solvable instances with its own number ranges, so these rates are for the uniform distribution rather than the benchmark's; the qualitative picture is what the method needs, and it holds with room to spare.

7.1 Try the oracle

This is the exact same dynamic program, in your browser. Enter numbers and a target, and every legal move is labeled the way the training reward would label it. Click a move to descend; the trail shows the residual distance \(d_y\) at each state.

viability oracle

8. Implementation notes

The oracle (countdown_oracle.py) exposes min_steps_to_target, is_alive and action_labels over canonicalized rational multisets. A step environment (countdown_step_env.py) parses the model's <step>a op b = c</step> strings, checks the arithmetic and the number usage, and attaches alive, distance_after and error metadata. Training alternates a vLLM sampling worker and a grouped policy-update worker; they cannot share the GPU, so the orchestrator kills one before creating the other and hands state across through checkpoints on disk. KL and entropy are estimated from sampled tokens only, since forming full vocabulary distributions over prompt tokens ran out of memory, and the loss supervises generated step tokens only.

The RLOO and IPO baselines are my own implementations too, built as milestones before VPO: IPO trained one epoch on 48k preference pairs with \(\beta=0.05\) (chosen over 0.1 because the smaller value pushes the loss target from 5 to 10 and measurably improved Pass@1), and RLOO for 100 steps of 128 prompts × 8 rollouts with a clipped sequence-level importance weight. Both were validated on the milestone test set before being used as comparators.

9. Limitations, stated plainly

  • VPO changes the reward interface, so it does not receive identical feedback to RLOO. The defensible claim is the narrower one: placing the reward at the step where solvability is decided gives a more accurate and much cheaper model on this task, which is why both the label budget and the token budget are reported rather than one number.
  • VPO-R uses the oracle at test time; it is an upper bound on what the viability signal can provide at inference. VPO-A is the fair comparison against SFT and IPO, and it does not beat RLOO on Pass@1.
  • Countdown admits an exact oracle. Elsewhere the alive predicate would come from a simulator, a constraint solver, or a learned critic, and the soundness theorem then holds only to the extent the approximation does.
  • The model is 0.5B parameters and the task is small; the results are about credit assignment, not about scale.

10. What I would do next

  • Approximate oracles. Replace the DP with a learned value head trained on oracle labels and measure how fast the theorems degrade as its accuracy drops; this is the bridge to tasks without an exact reachability predicate.
  • Distill the reranker into the policy. VPO-R shows the signal is there at inference; a second training phase that supervises the policy on the reranker's choices should close the 0.49 → 0.88 gap without an oracle at test time.
  • Harder state spaces. Sokoban-style puzzles and program synthesis with a type checker have exactly the legal-but-dead structure, with a cheap partial oracle.
  • Explain the repair collapse. The off-policy contamination story above is a hypothesis; an experiment that logs the importance ratio of inserted actions would settle it.

title: Blood and skin age prediction: what survives a new cohort?
desc: Built and stress-tested age-prediction models from public blood methylation and skin microbiome data. Follow the analysis from cohort curation and leakage checks to held-out predictions, missing-data failures, and the limits of combining unpaired biological measurements.
heroCaption: Held-out age predictions, independent-cohort failures and skin study-transfer error
body:
public-data research project · September 2026 · Python, scikit-learn, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib · 10 integrity checks

Can a model learn how old someone is from blood DNA methylation or the microbes on their skin—and still work when the next person comes from a different study? I revisited my 2023 age-prediction concept to answer that question with public data and an evaluation pipeline that makes its failures visible.

I assembled the cohorts, audited participant identities and assay quality, trained two independent prediction pipelines, and challenged their predictions with held-out participants, new studies, metadata baselines and shuffled labels. The most useful result was discovering which apparent gains depended on how the data were split.

The walkthrough: first establish who each sample belongs to; then build the clocks without leaking test data; compare their held-out predictions; and investigate why performance changes in a new cohort.

634
blood samples across two cohorts
1,798
skin samples / 339 participant IDs
3
figure sets, with code and results

Blood methylation predicted age with a 4.21-year mean absolute error under plate-held-out validation. Skin microbiome error was 9.17 years with participants held out and 18.35 years with studies held out. The central finding is the gap between learning age-associated patterns inside a cohort and generalizing to a new population.

The original abstract was titled Integration of Blood Methylome and Skin Microbiome Data in Machine Learning Algorithms for Accurate Age Prediction (W3PHIAI, Washington, DC, 2023; bibliographic record). Its original code and data were unavailable. Everything below is a newly executed 2026 analysis, not a recovered 2023 result. The public cohorts used here do not contain verified blood/skin measurements from the same people, so this project does not report a validated combined model or a multimodal accuracy gain.

Download code, results and figures · Metrics CSV · Data sources · Data audit

1. Start with the unit of evidence

I downloaded the released abundance matrix and metadata from Huang et al. and processed whole-blood methylation matrices from GEO. The methylation discovery cohort was GSE41037: 720 deposited samples, filtered to 360 healthy controls with the source's QC flag set to “yes” and age at least 18. The external cohort was GSE19711: 274 control women, with ages recorded at recruitment. Both matrices contained the same 27,578 CpG identifiers.

The skin matrix contained 1,975 samples and 7,311 ASVs, but only 340 study-qualified subject identifiers. In Qiita study 11052, all 177 rows had the same subject identifier while the age values included both 31 and 36. I excluded that identity-ambiguous study before model fitting, leaving 1,798 samples from 339 participant identifiers across three studies. Thirteen remaining participant identifiers had a one-year age difference across repeated samples. Those samples retained their recorded ages and stayed together in every participant-held-out split.

This is not a cosmetic distinction. Study 1841 supplies 1,293 samples from 83 participant identifiers, whereas study 10317 supplies 440 from 237. Counting each row equally would give the repeatedly sampled, predominantly younger cohort disproportionate influence. The skin models therefore receive inverse-sample-count training weights, and reported primary errors assign equal total weight to each participant.

2. Fit the models inside the validation loop

Blood methylation. Five outer folds held out entire assay plates; the eligible discovery samples occupied seven plates. Within each outer training set, three-fold plate-grouped validation selected 100 or 500 CpGs and ridge regularization α ∈ {10, 100, 1000}. Training-median imputation, age-correlation feature selection and standardization were refitted inside every inner fold. After internal evaluation, a final configuration was selected using only the discovery cohort and applied once to the external controls. No external ages were used for feature selection, fitting or calibration.

Skin microbiome. A sample-local Hellinger transformation (square root of relative abundance) followed training-only prevalence filtering at 1%. A 160-tree random forest used square-root feature subsampling; minimum leaf sizes of 1, 3 or 5 were selected inside three-fold participant-grouped validation. Five outer folds held out all samples from each test participant. The source table had already undergone age-independent prevalence filtering; this upstream, cohort-wide preprocessing could not be undone from the released processed matrix.

Controls. Training-age median baselines accompany both modalities. A study/site/sex-only ridge model tests how much age can be inferred from non-microbial metadata. A fixed forest with minimum leaf size 3 is evaluated under random-sample, participant-held-out and leave-one-study-out splits to isolate the consequences of changing the validation unit. Ten shuffled-label runs per modality refit preprocessing and models; skin labels are permuted at the participant level. A separate unshuffled run uses exactly the same model and target definition as each permutation control.

3. What the held-out predictions show

EvaluationSamplesMAE in years (95% interval)R²
Blood: plate-held-out nested CV3604.21 (3.78–4.50)0.91
Blood: independent cohort2746.03 (5.14–7.12)-1.38
Skin: participant-held-out nested CV1,7989.17 (8.39–9.92)0.44
Skin: study/site/sex only1,79810.06 (9.21–10.85)0.36
Skin: leave one study out, fixed RF1,79818.35 (17.12–19.65)-0.89

Blood MAE weights samples equally; skin MAE weights participants equally. Intervals use 2,000 resamples of plates for internal blood evaluation, samples for external blood evaluation, and participants for skin. They are conditional on the fitted predictions and do not include uncertainty from retraining. These are different cohorts and age distributions, so the table is not a controlled ranking of blood versus skin as biological modalities.

The blood model explains much of the age variation in plate-held-out discovery data (R² = 0.91). In external control women aged 52–78, MAE increases to 6.03 years and R² is -1.38. A negative external R² means that, under squared error, these predictions are worse than the constant external-cohort mean. The model still beats its training-median age baseline, but that baseline is weak under such a large age-distribution shift. Reporting only the favorable MAE comparison would hide this failure.

For skin, the metadata-only model gives 10.06-year MAE, versus 9.17 for the microbial model. The participant-bootstrap reduction is 0.89 years (95% conditional interval 0.46–1.32). Microbial features add information in these held-out participants, but study and demographic structure already explain a substantial portion of the predictive signal. The model increasingly underpredicts age in older participants.

4. Interrogate the failures

Repeated participants and study transfer

With random sample splitting, 90.5% of test samples have a participant represented in training. Both participant and study holdouts reduce that overlap to zero. For the fixed forest, participant-weighted MAE changes from 8.93 years under random sampling to 9.24 under participant holdout: an increase of 0.31 years, with a conditional participant-bootstrap interval of 0.15–0.48. The observed numerical difference is modest; the identity overlap is nevertheless a material difference in what the benchmark measures.

The larger effect is the evaluation population. For the same participant-held-out predictions, sample-weighted error is 6.44 years while participant-weighted error is 9.24 years. Leaving an entire study out raises the latter to 18.35 years. Study 1841 is largely young adults, and study 10317 covers a much broader, older population. The result is consistent with substantial cohort and age-distribution dependence, rather than a portable skin-aging clock. This is a new benchmark with different inclusion rules, transformations, weights and model settings; it is not a direct reproduction of the published study's headline accuracy.

Missing methylation measurements and implausible predictions

Two external controls have more than 1% missing CpGs. One has approximately 57% missing measurements and an unconstrained ridge prediction of −28.4 years at recorded age 74. The other large negative outlier is also highly incomplete. Predictions were neither clipped to plausible ages nor silently removed.

A post hoc quality sensitivity analysis applies a 1% missingness threshold to the locked external predictions: 272 samples remain, MAE becomes 5.48 years and R² remains -0.26. That check identifies an actionable assay-quality problem, but it does not rescue independent generalization and is not a replacement for the all-sample primary result. In deployment, a quality gate and an abstention policy would need to be specified and validated before use.

Feature interpretation and negative controls

The fitted blood ridge model assigns large standardized coefficients to CpGs annotated to NHLRC1, SCGN and ASPA; all three were selected in all five outer training sets. Coefficients are conditional on correlated features and the training scale, not causal effects of those genes. The full CpG list, coefficients and selection frequencies are downloadable. Skin impurity ranks include ASVs assigned to Mycoplasma, Enterobacteriaceae and other taxa. Those ranks are training-set summaries, can reflect cohort structure, and do not establish microbial drivers of aging. Taxonomic assignments come from the released annotation and are provisional, especially at species level.

Matched unshuffled models outperform the ten shuffled-label controls in each modality. This supports the presence of learnable age-associated structure in the chosen datasets. Ten permutations are a coarse diagnostic; they do not establish a high-resolution significance level or validate a mechanism.

5. Why these data do not validate integration

A genuine combined clock needs blood and skin measurements from the same participants, with outcomes held out at the participant level. Pairing unrelated people because their ages match would use the prediction target to manufacture the joint data. It could make an attractive scatterplot while answering a different, invalid question.

For a weighted average of two unbiased errors, its variance is

Var(w eblood + (1 − w)eskin) = w²σ²blood + (1 − w)²σ²skin + 2w(1 − w)Cov(eblood, eskin).

Separate cohorts do not identify that within-person covariance. Moreover, the observed marginal errors here come from different populations. They cannot be substituted into this expression to claim a measured fusion gain. I included a tested pairing utility that rejects disjoint participant IDs, duplicate participant rows and outcome columns among features. It is a guardrail for future paired data, not a trained or evaluated multimodal model.

6. What I learned—and what I would build next

The main deliverable is an auditable benchmark, with every held-out prediction available to inspect. A low average error alone is not enough: repeated participants change the evaluation unit, study composition changes who the model serves, and missing measurements can produce implausible ages. The external blood model still had negative R² after the exploratory quality filter, so removing the worst samples did not establish a portable clock.

For a next iteration, I would preregister assay-quality thresholds, test an abstention rule on a new cohort, and recruit paired blood and skin measurements with broad age coverage. Only then could a combined model be compared fairly with each single-modality clock, using participant-level splits and a truly untouched external cohort.

7. Explore the code and reproduce the analysis

The archive includes the executed analysis, derived predictions, metrics, data audit, annotation tables and all three figures as PNG, SVG and PDF. Source URLs are pinned to a Git commit for the microbial data, and every downloaded file has a SHA-256 checksum. Raw third-party matrices are retrieved by the download script rather than republished in the archive.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python src/download.py
python src/prepare.py
python src/analyze.py
python src/diagnostics.py
python src/figures.py
python src/test_analysis.py

The scientific integrity checks cover group separation, exclusion of the identity-ambiguous cohort, metric recomputation, external-control eligibility, and rejection of invalid cross-person fusion. A future extension should obtain a consented, paired cohort with synchronized sampling and verified participant IDs; predefine quality gates and holdouts; and compare each modality with a combined model on the same untouched participants.

Scope. These models estimate recorded chronological age. They have not been validated as biological-age, health-risk or clinical decision tools. Processed public data limit control over upstream normalization; participant identity is only as reliable as the deposited metadata; external blood age is recorded at recruitment; and three skin studies are too few to establish broad transportability. Figure quality does not change those evidential limits.

Sources

  1. Huang et al. Human Skin, Oral, and Gut Microbiomes Predict Chronological Age. mSystems (2020). Public matrix and metadata: author repository.
  2. Horvath et al. Aging effects on DNA methylation modules in human brain and blood tissue. Genome Biology (2012). Data: GSE41037.
  3. GSE19711, UK Ovarian Cancer Population Study whole-blood methylation data. This analysis uses control women only.
  4. GPL8490, Illumina HumanMethylation27 platform annotation.
  5. Scikit-learn grouped cross-validation documentation.
